Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel's Arab parties

By attacking Arab parties, Benjamin Netanyahu may be trying to ensure his main rival feels unable to consider forming a minority government with Arab help, analysts say.

JERUSALEM: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alleged on Thursday (Oct 29), without providing evidence, that Arab parties' record gains in an election this week were driven in part by voter fraud, a charge rejected by Arab leaders who accused the premier of incitement. The allegation represents an escalation of rhetoric against Arab parties by Netanyahu and his far-right partners after high Arab turnout in a national ballot on Tuesday effectively blocked a smooth path to power for either him or his main rivals. Israeli officials said on Thursday that the authorities were probing fraud allegations, though the election's integrity was not systematically compromised. Analysts and critics say that by stepping up attacks on Arab parties, Netanyahu may be trying to ensure his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, feels unable to even consider forming a minority government with Arab help that could oust him from power.

Netanyahu's goal is "delegitimising any Arab-Jewish cooperation", said Eytan Gilboa, professor of politics at Reichman University. Tuesday's tightly fought election has produced no clear winner and is likely to be followed by weeks of protracted negotiations over a new government. With nearly 99 per cent of votes counted, Netanyahu's nationalist-religious bloc held a modest lead in seats over a bloc of right-wing and centre-left parties led by Eisenkot, with both men's coalitions short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in parliament. Parties representing Israel's 21 per cent Arab minority were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Eisenkot's bloc, which has 48 seats against Netanyahu's camp of 53, with no path to power without broad Arab backing. Eisenkot has so far ruled out including the parties in government but his camp could try to form a minority government with Arab support from the outside.

Protesters sit on a road as they take part in a rally demanding that Israel-Arab parties in Israel be included in the formation of the next government coalition after yesterday's general election, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Oct 28, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Jamal Awad)

ELECTION INTEGRITY NOT SYSTEMATICALLY COMPROMISED, OFFICIALS SAY Ahmad Tibi, one of the leaders of the Arab Joint List party, said Netanyahu has launched a "toxic campaign" meant to undermine the election results. "This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra'am," Tibi told Reuters. During and after Tuesday's election, Netanyahu and his allies warned against rising Arab turnout and his right-wing Likud party issued statements accusing the Arab parties of "stealing the vote." It demanded police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service investigate incidents of suspected election bribery and intimidation at ballot stations in Arab towns. It said it possessed evidence of such activity but has not presented it to the public. The police say they have arrested at least seven people since Tuesday in Israel's south, where many Arabs live, on suspicion of voter fraud. On Thursday, the head of Israel's Central Election Committee, Supreme Court jurist Noam Sohlberg, said he had asked the Shin Bet to investigate suspicions that unidentified foreign players had tried to intervene in the election. Likud seized on Sohlberg's request, alleging an attack on Israel's democracy, "an Islamisation of Israel and the toppling of the right-wing in order to bring about IDF withdrawal and defeat on all fronts, foremost Iran". Likud said Qatar was behind the alleged election intervention, which Qatar denied. Ra'am head Mansour Abbas said his party was not involved and urged a full investigation. "We have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimisation he (Netanyahu) is waging against Arab citizens: Nothing will come of it, because there is nothing there," Abbas said in a statement. In a letter sent to a parliamentarian and published by the Central Election Committee, the committee said that there was "no base for claims that there was systematic harm to the election's integrity." Shin Bet said that its investigation was focused only on those involved and should not cast aspersions on "an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and legally."

"WE MUST NOT TARNISH AN ENTIRE COMMUNITY": ISRAELI PRESIDENT

The coalition that last toppled Netanyahu, in 2021, for the first time in Israel's history relied on an Arab party - Ra'am, which has Islamist roots. But Eisenkot's camp would need backing from the Arab-dominated Joint List, which includes an explicitly anti-Zionist party. Eisenkot said in a statement that the investigation into possible election meddling must be carried out without politicians intervening. "Likud and Netanyahu have set out on an orchestrated organised campaign to delegitimise the election results," Eisenkot said. After vote tallying is completed, President Isaac Herzog will consult with party chairs and choose a candidate who he thinks has the best chance to form a government. On Thursday, he said the allegations must be investigated. "But even at a moment like this, we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy," Herzog said.

Source: Reuters/ec

Moscow, Pyongyang back network sending workers to Russian factories: Report

The neighbours have boosted military and political ties dramatically since pledging renewed cooperation at a 2023 summit of their leaders.

SEOUL: A Russian network of brokers sponsored by Pyongyang has taken North Koreans to work in Russia in exploitative conditions and in violation of United Nations sanctions, some at factories that turn out items Moscow uses in the Ukraine war, a rights group said. The neighbours have boosted military and political ties dramatically since pledging renewed cooperation at a 2023 summit of their leaders, while a mutual defence pact is a cornerstone of a partnership treaty signed the following year. In its report, the Hague-based group, Global Rights Compliance (GRC), said North Korea reaps funds from the operation, taking much of the wages earned by its workers who are sent to Russia and made to stay under threat of retribution. The group cites open source information on the operation run by a Russian businessman, facial recognition technology to identify North Korean officials, and evidence gathered by its members posing undercover as prospective employers.

"This investigation exposes a dangerous convergence between two states' military ambitions," said the group's legal adviser, Elise Lauriot Prevost. These were "North Korea's use of overseas forced labour to finance its weapons programme, and Russia's growing reliance on labour to sustain its war economy," she added.

Russia's foreign ministry and the North Korean embassy in Moscow did not respond to emails seeking comment. The rights group said it contacted two Russians identified as key figures in the network, but only one replied, denying the accusation. It did not say if the other responded. NORTH KOREA SENT TROOPS, SOUTH SAYS Since 2024, North Korea has sent more than 10,000 troops to fight alongside Russians in the Ukraine war, as well as weapons to replenish Moscow's dwindling armoury while gaining valuable battlefield experience, South Korea's intelligence agency has said. To evade UN sanctions that ban member nations from hiring North Korean workers, the latter enter Russia on student visas in the guise of enrolling at colleges, GRC said. Then they are contracted out to Russian employers, with brokers receiving a commission of up to 150,000 roubles (US$1,860) for each, it added. GRC investigators posed undercover as prospective employers and found the workers were hired at production sites, including a military rations factory. The workers are forced to stay on the job through coercion and threats of retribution against them and their families. One advertisement assured prospective employers that workers would not "run away," the report said. Workers labour 12-hour days with two days off each month, it added, citing such ads.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as they attend a ceremony to mark the 80th anniversary of the end of World War Two, in Beijing, China, in this picture released by the Korean Central News Agency on Sep 4, 2025. (File photo: Reuters)

After North Korea's sixth and last nuclear test in 2017, a UN Security Council resolution put a blanket ban on the hiring of its workers overseas and mandated their return home. Russia and China, two permanent members of the Security Council that voted for the ban, have since been accused by South Korea and the West of noncompliance with resolutions. Such measures, dating back to 2006, banned the flow of goods, energy, weapons and workers with North Korea. In previous years, Russia employed North Korean labourers in its far east while many North Koreans staffing restaurants in China sent home wages that were channelled to the state treasury, rights groups have said. North Korea is directly involved in running the network supplying workers in Russia, with officials from its Moscow embassy identified as inspecting work sites for prospective employment, the GRC report said. "These workers do not come cheap, yet little, if any, of the money paid for their labour reaches them," said Dyland Carter, a GRC lead investigator. "Instead, it lines the pockets of the DPRK state," he added, referring to North Korea by a short version of its official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
